set.st: An 1874 letter from Gorton L. Scott, left in charge of the Ottawa House after the Port Sheldon land bubble burst, says two strangers who stopped there one October night were murdered by 'Irish Mike' and Dennis, and their bodies and 'some of the plunder' were buried 'near the run at the base of the blow-hole, just west of the hotel'. Scott searched about 1871, but 'shifting sands' had changed the bluffs. By 1899 every vestige of Port Sheldon was gone and strangers were seen surveying and digging there (Grand Haven Tribune); the hotel's shore is still unconfirmed. Pin is the townsite at the lake outlet, not the spot.

set.st: When the 1830s Port Sheldon land-company city failed, 'one of the capitalists buried what money he had' to keep it from the receivers. 'The shifting sands covered the spot', and though he 'searched for many a day' the money eluded him. In 1921 the Ottawa House hotel site was still marked by the decayed maples of its avenue; its lumber went into a barn E of the Grand Rapids Boy Scout camp. The earliest printed notice of digging is 1899: the Grand Haven Tribune said every vestige of old Port Sheldon was gone and 'mysterious men' spent days 'surveying and digging' there, 'maybe some of the gold ... is still hidden in the sands'. Pin is the townsite, not a spot.
set.t: Single 1921 magazine telling; no period record yet. Shifting dune sand. Township park and private dune lots: permission; the power-plant land is excluded. By 1913 one red building, then a barn, alone remained, and 'the lighthouse and harbor bell are now buried under the shifting sand dunes': the 1830s lighthouse site at the Pigeon Lake entrance lies under the dunes, a sign of how deep the drift is over the townsite. Strangers were seen digging there by 1899; no find reported. See also the Ottawa House murder-plunder card: the 1895 Detroit News piece on this dead town links other dark deeds to 'the old Scare Valley house'.

src: Grand Haven Tribune, 3 and 5 Feb 1897, p. 1 (Ottawa House register, 1838-40)

set.st: Old Niles people said the French fort just above the dam (Fort St. Joseph) was massacred by Indians, and that gold was thrown into the fort's well and more buried on the river bank. The fort stood 'up the river from Niles, near a mile'; its well was 'near two crab apple trees' older residents remembered, and 'a large amount of French sovereigns' were thrown in, but floods soon filled it and it was never found. The last to hunt for it was the late Robert Chambers, 'who tilled the premises'. Elliot H. Crane collected silver buttons, bracelets and crucifixes on the site and sold them to the Northern Indiana Historical Society. The late Ransom Dopp (a stage driver in 1848, later owner of about 1,500 acres in Wayne Twp, Cass Co) was rumoured to have found the bank cache: he was seen digging on the river bank, stopped suddenly, and then bought a large tract. The Dowagiac Republican, answering, said his neighbours doubted it. The Niles editor had heard the tale more than 50 years earlier from the Indian Bertrand. In Dec 1898, answering the Chicago Chronicle's Bertrand story, the Niles Daily Star had already noted that locals told of a large sum buried 'just above the dam in this city' in the French and Indian war.
pinev: 1889 Sanborn, Niles, sheet 6: DAM across the St Joseph between the Michigan Wood Pulp Co. and the Ohio Paper Co. mills, '3/4 mile S. of Main St'.

2015 1 m LiDAR: the flattened river surface steps up about 4.2 m (194.7 m to 198.9 m) at about 41.8175, -86.2588, which is the dam; pin about 150 m upstream of it. Moved from a pin about 2 km north, off the river.
The 1899 account places the fort 'just above the dam', matching the Fort St. Joseph site on the E bank upstream of the dam; pin unchanged.
'Near a mile' up river from Niles (May 1899) = the Fort St. Joseph site; pin unchanged.
1899: the fort site given as one mile south of Niles on the east bank, matching the pin above the dam.
